extraction.segment_function: Analyze the contradictions in Locke, Smith, and Marx regarding labor, distinguishing between labor and work, and highlighting Marx's foundational contradiction between glorifying labor and seeking emancipation from it.

claims.claim: Locke had to introduce money as a lasting thing to allow the laboring body to become the origin of property, because labor naturally produces only things of short duration.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Thus Locke, in order to save labor from its manifest disgrace of producing only “things of short duration,” had to introduce money—a “lasting thing which men may keep without spoiling”—a kind of deus ex machina without which the laboring body, in its obedience to the life process, could never have become the origin of anything so permanent and lasting as property

claims.claim: Marx's thought contains a fundamental contradiction wherein he defines man as an animal laborans while maintaining that human emancipation requires liberation from labor rather than its glorification.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The fact remains that in all stages of his work he defines man as an animal laborans and then leads him into a society in which this greatest and most human power is no longer necessary. We are left with the rather distressing alternative between productive slavery and unproductive freedom.

definitions.definition: A term used by Marx to define man through labor as an eternal necessity imposed by nature.

distinctions.distinction: The proportion between what nature gives and what man adds is opposite in the products of labor and work; consumption goods never completely lose their naturalness (e.g., grain in bread), whereas work reifies and creates an objective world of things where the raw material disappears.

must_not_be_lost: Locke's reliance on money to bridge the gap between ephemeral labor and durable property
Marx's contradiction between labor as human essence and the political goal of emancipating man from labor
